christmas-lights.meta: Christmas lights at Lake Cherokee, TX: custom-cut C9 roofline lights on the road side and water side, taken down and stored. Most homes start at $900.
christmas-lights.h1: Christmas lights for Lake Cherokee houses
christmas-lights.lede: Custom-cut C9 roofline lights for Lake Cherokee homes, with the road side, the water side or both lit, then taken down in January and stored.
christmas-lights.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes hangs professional Christmas lights at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We supply the lights, custom-cut C9 lines to your roofline, install them, take them down in January and store them. Most homes start at $900, quoted from a photo mock-up. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
christmas-lights.local_h: Lighting both faces of a lake house
local: Lake houses are built to be seen from two directions. A Lake Cherokee home often has long rooflines, gables and porches on the road side and again on the water side. That gives you a choice that a street-facing house does not have. We can outline the road side, the water side or both, and each shows up on the photo mock-up we quote from, so you pick before you book.

Quoting is done from photos, and because Lake Cherokee is a short drive from Longview, a house here is priced like most homes close to our base. Most start at $900, and installs more than an hour out start at $1,800, which does not apply here. Size of the house, how much roofline you want lit and any extras set the final number. The mock-up shows the design and the price together.

Each run is measured and each C9 line is cut to fit, so the light follows the gables and ridges with no gaps. We hang them with clips that do not damage shingles, on timers, with weatherproof connections. Pines and hardwoods close to a lake house are good candidates for tree wraps, and ground stakes, garland and wreaths are options. Warm white, full color or a custom mix. Tell us the color you want before the mock-up is built.

The rest of the job is ours. If a section goes out in December, tell us and we come back. In January we take it all down and store it for next year, so there is no tangled box to fight in the attic. Booking opens in early October, installs run through Thanksgiving week, and the calendar fills fast. A short drive makes the date easy to set. Lock your date early and you get the slot you want.

Trees are the thing to mention when you send photos. Include the whole front of the house with the pines and hardwoods in the frame, and tell us which ones you want wrapped. Ground stakes, garland and wreaths add to the price, and the mock-up shows exactly what is included before you book. Return clients who reuse the same install get a discounted rate, so the first season sets up the next one.

faq.q: Can you light the lake side of the house?
faq.a: Yes. We can outline the roofline on the road side, the water side or both. Each side shows up on the photo mock-up we quote from, so you can pick before you book. The mock-up shows each option with its price, so you can compare lighting one side against both.

faq.q: How much do Christmas lights cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most homes start at $900. Final price depends on the size of the house, how much of the roofline and property you want lit, and any extras like tree wraps or garland. The photo mock-up shows what is included. Once you approve the mock-up, nobody has to stand in your yard waiting on a ladder for a price.

faq.q: Do I need to meet anyone before I get a quote?
faq.a: No. Send photos of the house, ideally from both the road and the water side, and we build a mock-up and quote from that. After you approve, we measure each run and custom-cut the lines. Each year the same install can be reused, and return clients get a discounted rate on it.

faq.q: What happens if a section goes out mid-season?
faq.a: Service calls during the season are part of the job. Tell us which section is out and we come back to fix it. In January we take everything down and store it. Mid-season service calls are included, so you are not left fixing a dark section yourself.

faq.q: When should I book?
faq.a: As early as you can. Booking opens in early October, installs run through Thanksgiving week, and the calendar fills up fast. Getting your date locked early gets you the slot you want. A short drive from Longview makes Lake Cherokee easy to fit on the calendar, but the slots still go.

drainage.title: Lake Cherokee Drainage & Erosion Fixes | Yard Dog Landscapes
drainage.meta: Drainage and erosion fixes at Lake Cherokee, TX: swales, French drains, downspout runs. Small fixes from $450, most lake lot projects $2,000 to $3,750.
drainage.h1: Drainage that stops lake lot washouts
drainage.lede: Water on a Lake Cherokee lot always heads downhill. We give it a controlled path so it leaves without taking the yard with it.
drainage.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes fixes drainage at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We trace where the water comes from, then regrade, reroute downspouts, cut swales or install French drains. Most projects run $2,000 to $3,750, and small fixes start around $450. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews. Ask for a free walkthrough.
drainage.local_h: Getting water down a slope without cutting a gully
local: On a flat lot the question is where the water pools. On a Lake Cherokee lot the question is how fast it moves. Rain runs across the lawn, picks up sandy topsoil and cuts ruts along drives and paths. We start by watching it when we can, during or right after a rain, tracing where it comes from and where it ends up. Then we pick the fix. That watching is a free part of the walkthrough.

The tools are swales, French drains, downspout runs and dry creek beds, used together. A swale slows water on the surface. A French drain, with sock-wrapped pipe in #57 stone, carries it underground past the house. Downspouts get solid pipe, not a splash block. Every run needs a real outlet lower on the lot, released slowly enough that it does not cut a new gully. We work out that outlet before we price the job.

Walls and drains go together. The July 2026 driveway wall we rebuilt at Lake Cherokee has drainage fabric and pipe behind it plus a gravel drain strip along the drive, because a wall with no water path leans. Any retaining wall we build gets the same. Where a bank is washing, erosion control means grading, plus a bed, ground cover or sod on the bare soil. A wall and its drain are one job.

Price follows pipe length, dig depth and the outlet. Small fixes like a downspout reroute run $450 to $1,000. A standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500. Most lake lot projects fall between $2,000 and $3,750. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch, but a drain done before the spring rains saves another wet season. Combined work, like a wall and drainage together, runs $4,500 and up.

Timing is mostly about seeing the problem. A call right after a hard rain lets us watch where the water goes and what it carries. Dry weather makes the digging go faster, since saturated clay is heavy and sticky. Once the pipe is in, we cap the trench with soil and sod, or finish it in river rock or a dry creek bed. On a bank, sod or rock on top keeps the trench from becoming the next washout.

faq.q: Where does the water go on a Lake Cherokee drainage job?
faq.a: Downhill, on a controlled path. We collect runoff from roofs, drives and the slope above, carry it in pipe or a rock-lined swale past the house and walls, and release it lower on the lot slowly enough that it does not cut a new gully.

faq.q: Can you stop my yard from washing out?
faq.a: Usually, with the right mix. We slow the water with grading and swales, carry it with French drains, hold steep ground with walls or terraces and cover bare soil with beds, ground cover or sod. Walking the lot tells us which of those it takes. Often it is a combination, which is why most jobs run $2,000 to $3,750.

faq.q: How much does drainage work cost?
faq.a: Most projects run $2,000 to $3,750. A downspout reroute or one low spot runs $450 to $1,000. A single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, and large or combined projects run $4,500 and up. You get an itemized estimate in writing.

faq.q: When is the best time to look at my drainage problem?
faq.a: During or right after a rain, when we can see where the water really goes. We fix drainage year-round, and digging is easier in a dry stretch, so you do not have to wait for the perfect day to call.

faq.q: Do you handle drainage behind retaining walls?
faq.a: Yes, and every wall we build has it. A gravel chimney, perforated drain and outlet go behind the block so pressure never builds. A wall without it is the one that ends up leaning. On the Lake Cherokee driveway wall, that drainage is what the rebuild was missing.

fertilization.title: Lake Cherokee Lawn Fertilization | Yard Dog Landscapes
fertilization.meta: Lawn fertilization at Lake Cherokee, TX. Soil test first, slow-release feedings timed to the forecast, kept off drives and the shore. From about $190 a visit.
fertilization.h1: Fertilizing lawns on Lake Cherokee lots
fertilization.lede: A soil test, slower-release products and careful timing, so the feeding stays in the lawn at Lake Cherokee and does not run down the slope.
fertilization.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes fertilizes Lake Cherokee lawns from our Longview base, a short drive southeast. We soil test first, then follow a written schedule of slow-release feedings, with core aeration for compacted turf. Visits start from about $190 depending on lawn size and rounds. The plan and price come in writing before the first application. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
fertilization.local_h: Feeding a lawn that sits above the water
local: Fertilizer behaves differently on a lake lot. Put it on a slope right before a downpour and it does not feed the lawn. It rides the runoff down the bank, and some of it ends up in the water. So the plan at Lake Cherokee starts with a soil test, which tells us what the grass needs instead of what a bag label suggests. We use slower-release products, keep the spreader off the drive and away from the shoreline, and watch the forecast before every visit.

The sandy topsoil common around the lake drains fast and holds little. That makes timing matter more. Our first feeding goes down around the end of April, once overnight lows hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. A second goes down in early July, a third in early September, and October is a potassium-heavy winterizer. Nitrogen in March mostly washes away, and a late heavy dose only feeds soft growth that frost burns off.

Years of pine needles and acidic rain tend to leave East Texas soil a little low on pH. Under the pines around the lake, the test may say lime. When it does, lime goes into the plan. Compacted ground gets core aeration between late August and mid-September, which lets water soak in on the gentler grades instead of sheeting across the top, and the feeding follows right behind it. Test results go in the written plan, so you can see why each product is there.

Thin grass on a steep bank is a different case. More fertilizer will not fix turf that is shaded out or sliding. If the test and the walk-through say the problem is shade or slope, we will tell you that, and point you toward a bed or ground cover. Feedings start from about $190 per visit, and the plan comes before the first application. A thick, healthy lawn on the gentle grades also helps hold the soil in place.

faq.q: Is it safe to fertilize a lawn on a lake lot?
faq.a: Yes, when it is done carefully. We soil test so we only apply what the lawn needs, use slower-release products, keep the spreader off drives and away from the shoreline, and time feedings so a storm does not wash them off the slope.

faq.q: What does lawn fertilization cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. Seasonal programs are priced on lawn size, grass type and how many rounds the lawn needs, and lime or aeration add to it when the test calls for them. You see the plan and price in writing first.

faq.q: When do you fertilize in East Texas?
faq.a: Around April 25 for the first feeding, early July for the second, early September for the last real nitrogen, and an October winterizer high in potassium. We skip the early spring rush because the grass cannot use it yet. The written plan shows the date for each round and what goes down, so nothing is a surprise.

faq.q: Do you include weed or pest treatments in the program?
faq.a: No. We do not offer chemical treatments of any kind. Our work is soil testing, fertilizer, lime and core aeration, plus advice on mowing height and watering that keeps a lawn thick enough to crowd weeds out on its own.

faq.q: Should I aerate a sloped lawn?
faq.a: On compacted ground, yes, between late August and mid-September. The holes let water soak in instead of running off. We feed right after, and we skip aerating anywhere the ground is too steep or loose to work safely. Steep banks are usually better as beds or ground cover, which need no feeding program.

flower-bed-installation.title: Lake Cherokee Flower Beds & Ground Cover | Yard Dog
flower-bed-installation.meta: Flower bed installation at Lake Cherokee, TX. Beds built across the slope, edged on the low side and planted with ground cover that grips. $900 to $3,600.
flower-bed-installation.h1: Flower beds and ground cover on Lake Cherokee slopes
flower-bed-installation.lede: On a Lake Cherokee lot, a bed is often the best answer for ground too steep to mow. We build them to stay where they are put.
flower-bed-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes installs flower beds at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We cut and edge the bed, pull weeds by the root, amend the soil, plant perennials, shrubs and ground cover, and mulch at 1 to 1.5 inches. Most planting projects run $900 to $3,600. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
flower-bed-installation.local_h: Beds that hold a bank and still look good
local: The first question on a lake lot is whether the bed can hold. A bed built straight down a slope funnels water into a channel. We build across the slope instead, so each row slows the run. The low side gets a firm edge in stone, steel or a clean natural cut, which keeps soil and mulch from sliding. That is the difference between a bed that settles in and one that ends up in the yard below.

The plants do the long-term holding. Asian jasmine, liriope and monkey grass spread and grip soil well in East Texas, and they handle the shade under pines. We plant them in amended soil, mulch them and let them fill in. Shrubs go in where roots can brace the bank, and perennials go where sun reaches. Sun-lovers like lantana, salvia and knockout roses are saved for the spots that really get six hours.

Timing helps the roots. Plant in fall, September through November, or early spring, and the roots get a season to grab hold before summer. Heat lovers like vinca wait for warm soil, usually mid-May and later. The sandy topsoil common around the lake drains quickly, but whatever clay sits below it holds water, so we tell you to water deep and less often. Daily watering in clay is how good plants get killed.

Planning and price are straightforward. You get a written estimate with plant counts, sizes and the edging spec. If you want to see it drawn first, our $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering. Most planting projects run $900 to $3,600, and a small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. The estimate usually follows the walkthrough within a day, with the plant list itemized.

Shade changes the plant list. Under the pines at Lake Cherokee, azaleas and hydrangeas work only where they are sited right, out of the worst afternoon heat. Sunnier spots near the drive can take heat-tolerant plants. Before we decide on a single plant, we check how many hours of sun each bed gets, how it drains after a rain and what you want to see from the porch. Plants go in with real spacing so air moves through them.

faq.q: What ground covers hold a lake slope?
faq.a: Asian jasmine, liriope and monkey grass spread and hold soil well in East Texas, and they handle shade under pines. We plant them in amended soil and mulch them until they fill in. On a bank they also protect the soil year-round, since the roots stay in place after the leaves drop.

faq.q: Why do you build beds across the slope?
faq.a: Rows across the grade slow water down. A bed running straight downhill acts like a ditch. Across the slope, with an edge on the low side, soil and mulch stay put and rain has time to soak in. It is the same logic as a terrace, only softer and cheaper than a wall.

faq.q: How much does a flower bed cost?
faq.a: New beds are priced with our landscaping and planting work, most projects $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size, plant choices, edging and soil prep set the number. We itemize all of it in writing.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant?
faq.a: Fall, September through November, while the soil is warm and the air is cooling. Early spring works too. Heat lovers like vinca should wait until the soil is truly warm, mid-May or later. Fall is easiest because the roots get months to settle in before summer heat.

faq.q: Can I see the bed before you plant?
faq.a: Yes. Our $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering first. It is a separate fee, so you can decide on the install once you have seen the plan. It is optional, and you can go straight to the written estimate and plant list instead.

hardscaping.title: Lake Cherokee Patios, Paths & Steps | Yard Dog Landscapes
hardscaping.meta: Patios, walkways and steps at Lake Cherokee, TX, built on a compacted base that handles the grade. Most hardscape projects run $3,100 to $9,100.
hardscaping.h1: Patios, paths and steps for Lake Cherokee slopes
hardscaping.lede: Level ground, safe steps and walkways that hold up on a lot that tilts to the water, built on a base that does not move.
hardscaping.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes builds patios, walkways, steps and fire pits at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We dig out, compact the base and pitch every surface to shed water. Most projects run $3,100 to $9,100, set by square footage, material and how the site sits. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
hardscaping.local_h: Making flat ground where the lot does not have any
local: A patio needs level ground, and a lake lot does not have much. So the first job is cut and fill. We dig into the slope on the high side, build up the low side and, where it needs holding, put in a short wall. The result is a flat pad where there was a tilted lawn. A patio set on a thin bed of sand over a slope will rock and shift, so the base is not where we save money.

Underneath, the ground moves. Sandy loam over red clay swells after heavy spring rain and shrinks in a dry August. We excavate to depth, compact a crushed stone base and pitch the surface away from the house. On a lake lot the pitch has a second job, since water that runs under a patio undermines it. Where a patio sits at the bottom of a grade, we plan the drainage before we set the first paver.

Getting down to the water is the other half. We build steps in block or natural stone on a compacted base, so they do not shift, and a flagstone or paver walk beside them. Paired with a short wall or terraced beds, they turn a slope you avoid into one you use. Docks and boathouses are not our work. The walk to them, up to the bank, is. That includes the landing at the top and the bottom, so you are not stepping onto soft ground.

Material changes the number. Pavers, flagstone and chopped stone all price differently, and walls, steps and fire features add to it. If you want to see the layout first, our $449 Hardscape Preview gives you renderings. Most projects run $3,100 to $9,100, and you get an itemized written estimate after we walk the site. Fire pits, seating walls and outdoor kitchens are priced the same way, by material and size, and each is itemized.

Spring and fall book up first, though we build patios year-round. Base work goes best in a dry stretch, because saturated clay will not compact, so a rainy week can move a dig day. If you want to be sitting on it by a certain season, call a few weeks ahead. When the build is done we fill the joints, restore the ground around the work and haul off the spoil, which on a slope is a lot of dirt.

faq.q: Can you build steps down a Lake Cherokee slope?
faq.a: Yes. We build steps in block or natural stone on a compacted base so they do not shift. Paired with a short wall or terraced beds, they turn a slope you avoid into one you use. We pitch each tread slightly so rain runs off, and we base them on compacted stone, not loose soil.

faq.q: How much does a patio cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most hardscape projects run $3,100 to $9,100. A small patio or walkway lands at the low end, and a large outdoor living build costs more. Material, square footage, excavation and walls or steps all move it. A written, itemized estimate comes after we walk the site and see the grade.

faq.q: How do you level a patio on a slope?
faq.a: Cut and fill. We dig into the high side, build up the low side and hold it with a short wall where needed, then compact a crushed stone base and pitch the surface to shed water. The fill is compacted in layers before anything is built on top of it.

faq.q: Will a patio settle on this soil?
faq.a: Not if the base is right. Clay moves, so we dig out to depth, compact the base in layers and plan the drainage. Settling usually comes from a thin base and water getting underneath. We would rather spend the extra day on the base than come back to a patio that rocks.

faq.q: Can I see the layout before you build?
faq.a: Yes. The $449 Hardscape Preview gives you layout renderings first. It is a separate fee, and you can decide on the build afterward. A hardscape preview is useful when a patio, steps and a wall all have to fit one sloped space, because you see how they sit together before any dirt moves.

hedge-trimming.title: Lake Cherokee Hedge Trimming Without Losing Your View | Yard Dog
hedge-trimming.meta: Hedge trimming at Lake Cherokee, TX by hand. Screens held at the height you pick, clippings hauled off the slope. Most hedge jobs run $150 to $800.
hedge-trimming.h1: Hedge trimming for Lake Cherokee homes
hedge-trimming.lede: Hedges trimmed to screen the road or the neighbors without closing off the water, with every clipping hauled off the slope.
hedge-trimming.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes trims hedges and shrubs at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We shape by hand, from routine trims to hard rejuvenation cuts, and haul off every clipping. Most jobs run $150 to $800 depending on the number of shrubs, their size and how overgrown they are. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
hedge-trimming.local_h: Screening the road without hiding the water
local: On a lake lot, a hedge usually has two jobs. It screens the road or the next house, and it has to leave the water visible. Those goals pull against each other as a hedge grows. Give us a view line from the porch or the deck and we will hold the hedge at the height that blocks the neighbor and not the lake. We trim to that line every visit, so the view does not creep shut over a summer.

Hedge work at the lake produces a lot of debris, and where it lands matters. Clippings left on a bank wash into the slope or lodge against a wall. We put tarps down under the work, rake up what falls and haul off all of it. The beds get blown clean and the walks swept before we leave. Nothing gets left on the lot for the next rain to move around.

How we cut depends on the shrub. Hollies, yaupons and boxwoods are forgiving and shape well in June. Azaleas and mophead hydrangeas set next year's buds on this year's stems, so they wait until right after bloom. We shape each hedge a little wider at the base so the lower branches keep their leaves. A bare-legged hedge is common on shaded lots. Before we cut anything we count the shrubs and note which ones bloom on old wood.

Shade under the pines makes shrubs lean toward the light, and the open side of the plant often grows fastest. Most hedges here want two to three trims between spring and fall, and we can set you on a recurring schedule or come back when you call. Skip hard shearing in late fall, because tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. Jobs mostly run $150 to $800. Tell us which shrubs you have and we will plan the timing for each.

Price follows the shrubs, not the lake. A handful of foundation shrubs by the front door sits at the low end of the range, and a long, tall screen along the road side costs more. Formal shaping, topiary and a heavy load of debris push it up as well. We count the shrubs at the walkthrough, check which ones bloom on old wood and send an itemized price in writing, usually within a day. Lake Cherokee is a short run from Longview, so setting up a recurring trim schedule is easy.

faq.q: Can you trim a hedge without blocking my lake view?
faq.a: Yes. Show us where the view line is and we will hold the hedge at a set height so it screens the road or a neighbor without cutting off the water. We trim to that same line each visit. If a shrub has outgrown the line, we can cut it back hard once and hold it from then on.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. A handful of foundation shrubs sits at the low end. Long, tall or badly overgrown hedges cost more. You get an itemized price in writing, usually within a day of the walkthrough. Formal shaping or topiary work costs more than a natural-form trim.

faq.q: Do you haul away the clippings?
faq.a: Always. We put tarps down, rake up every clipping and haul it away. On a sloped lot that matters, because trimmings left on a bank wash downhill or end up against a wall. The beds and walks are blown clean before we leave, so you do not find leaf litter on the drive the next morning.

faq.q: How often should a lake lot hedge be trimmed?
faq.a: Most want two to three trims a season, in the stretch from spring to fall when they grow fastest. Fast growers along the sunny side of the house may want more. We can schedule recurring visits or come back when you call.

faq.q: My hedge is badly overgrown. Can it be saved?
faq.a: Often. Hard rejuvenation cuts bring many overgrown shrubs back, and we know which kinds take it well. We tell you at the walkthrough if a shrub is better replaced than cut back. Some shrubs do not recover from a hard cut, and being honest about that saves you money.

irrigation.title: Lake Cherokee Sprinkler Systems & Repair | Yard Dog Landscapes
irrigation.meta: Sprinkler system installation and repair at Lake Cherokee, TX, zoned for slopes, under a Texas licensed irrigator. Permits pulled, free walkthrough.
irrigation.h1: Sprinkler systems zoned for Lake Cherokee slopes
irrigation.lede: New sprinkler systems and repairs for Lake Cherokee yards, with the slope zoned on its own so water soaks in and does not run to the shore.
irrigation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes installs and repairs sprinkler systems at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. Irrigation work is done under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657, who checks every system, and we pull the permits the job requires. Pricing comes after a free walkthrough. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
irrigation.local_h: Watering a yard that falls to the water
local: A sprinkler that runs too long on a Lake Cherokee lot just sends the runoff down the bank. Flat ground by the house takes a long cycle fine. A slope does not, because the water runs off before it soaks in. So we zone the slope separately from the level ground, and run shorter cycles on it that let the water sink in. That keeps the high side from drying out and the low side from flooding.

Sand on top and clay underneath makes this worse. The sandy topsoil takes water fast and dries fast, then the clay below stops it and pushes it sideways. Short cycles, spaced out, work with that. Sun and shade get their own zones too, since the grass under the pines drinks less than the open yard. We lay out the zones around how the yard behaves, not around one big loop.

Beds and banks go on drip. Spray heads in a bed soak the leaves, the mulch and the side of the house and still leave the roots thirsty. Drip puts the water at the roots and keeps foliage dry, which matters with the fungus that shows up in a wet, warm spring. On a bank planted in ground cover, drip also keeps water from running off the surface. Drip also stops overspray on drives and walks.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work. Our systems are designed and installed under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657. City-water systems get a backflow device, new automatic systems get a rain or freeze sensor, and we check what your address requires and pull the permit. We serve both the Gregg and Rusk sides of the lake. Spring and fall are the best install windows, and repairs happen year-round. Pricing comes after a free walkthrough, with the quote itemized in writing.

Freeze season needs a plan. Before the first hard freeze, make sure the system has a working freeze sensor or is shut off, and check every zone again when you turn it back on in spring. We program the controller for the season and show you how to change it, so you are not watering in the rain. Every zone is run and adjusted for coverage, and the licensed irrigator checks the system before we call it done.

faq.q: Do you install sprinkler systems at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Yes. We install and repair sprinkler systems on both the Gregg County and Rusk County sides of the lake, under a Texas licensed irrigator. Sloped lake lots get zoned so water soaks in instead of running to the shoreline. Priced after a free walkthrough, with the zones planned around your slope.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost?
faq.a: It depends on how much of the yard you want watered, how many zones that takes, whether beds need drip and your water source. We price after a free walkthrough and send a written, itemized quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: Can you fix a system you did not install?
faq.a: Yes. We fix broken heads and lines, leaking valves, zones that will not come on, bad wiring and heads watering the street, on systems we put in and systems we did not. Controllers nobody has set since the house was built get reset too.

faq.q: Do I need a permit?
faq.a: Many East Texas cities require one for a new system, and the rules vary. We check what your address requires and pull the permit before we dig. Rules differ by city and county, and the lake straddles a county line, so we check the address rather than assume.

faq.q: Should my banks and beds be on drip?
faq.a: Almost always. Drip puts water at the roots, wastes almost none and keeps foliage dry. On a slope, it also keeps water from running off the surface the way spray does. Spray heads work fine on open turf, where we space them for full coverage.

landscaping.local_h: A planting plan that works with the grade
local: Landscaping on a lake lot starts with the slope. A flat yard asks what you would like to see. A Lake Cherokee yard asks what is going to stay put. We walk the lot first, noting sun, shade, grade and where water runs after a rain, then lay out options in writing. The plan works with the fall of the land instead of fighting it: level spots made with walls or terraces, beds planted across the grade and steps where you need a way down.

Beds do the work that turf cannot. On banks too steep or shaded to mow, we put in shrubs, perennials and ground covers with roots that grip. Plantings go across the slope, not up and down it, so mulch and soil are held on the low side by an edge. A bed on the shaded side of a pine fills in slower, so we choose plants for the hours of light they will really get.

Paths matter too. A trail to the water that washes out every spring is only a ditch. We build walks and flagstone stepping-stone paths on a base that stays put, pitched so they shed water. Where grade change is steep, we step the path or add a short wall. Retaining walls and drainage are part of our landscaping scope, so a plan can include them without bringing in anyone else.

Fall is the best planting window in East Texas, from September to about Thanksgiving, because roots build for months before they meet summer heat. If you would like to see the plan drawn first, a full-property Design Preview is $999, credited toward the install if you book within 90 days. Most projects land between $900 and $3,600, from small refreshes to full front and back yard installs. Walking the lot together is free, and the written plan usually follows within a day.

Cleanup and aftercare close it out. Trees and shrubs go in with the root flare at grade, never buried, then the beds get mulch or rock and a clean edge. We haul off the debris, blow off the walks and drive, and go over how to water the new plants through their first season. Deep and less often is the rule, because clay holds water for days after a soaking rain and plants die from wet feet as often as from drought.

faq.q: How do you landscape a lot that slopes to the lake?
faq.a: We work with the slope: walls or terraces to create level spots, beds planted across the grade, paths with steps, and drainage that carries water down in a controlled way. We walk the lot first and lay out the options in writing.

faq.q: What does landscaping cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most projects run $900 to $3,600. Small bed refreshes start at a few hundred dollars, and large custom designs cost more. Plant count, materials, soil work and add-ons like walls, sod or drainage all move the number. You see the itemized number in writing before any work starts.

faq.q: Can I see the design before you start?
faq.a: Yes. A full-property Design Preview is $999 and shows renderings before anything goes in the ground. If you book the install within 90 days, the fee is credited toward it. The preview is optional, and you can book straight from the written estimate.

faq.q: Do you build docks or work at the shoreline?
faq.a: No. Docks, boathouses and seawalls are not our work. We stay on the land side and handle the yard from the house down, including walls, beds, paths and drainage. If your plan touches the water's edge, we will point you to a contractor who specializes in shoreline structures.

faq.q: Do you do all the work yourselves?
faq.a: Yes. Miller and the same crew of four do every job, and we never subcontract. The people who walked your lot are the people who build the plan. You get the same people from walkthrough to final cleanup, and a written, itemized estimate in between.

lawn-maintenance.local_h: Mowing a yard that runs down to the water
local: A Lake Cherokee yard rarely sits flat. Most lots fall to the shore, so one property can hold a level patch by the house, a gentle grade below it and a bank that drops off near the water. We mow the level ground and the easy grades with the deck and pace set for the footing. The steep stretch gets string-trimmed instead, because a mower on a wet bank is a bad idea for the machine and the person pushing it. You get a flat per-visit price in writing before the first cut.

Clippings matter more on a slope than on a town lot. Blown downhill, they end up against a wall, in a drain inlet or along the shoreline. We blow them back onto the lawn and clean the drive and walks, so nothing travels down the lot after the next rain. Early fall leaves are handled the same way, mulched into the turf with the mower while the drop is still light.

Shade under the pines and hardwoods decides how each part of the yard is cut. Sunny bermuda runs about one to one and a half inches in spring and two to two and a half in summer. Shaded St. Augustine stays at three and a half to four inches all summer. Where both grow in one yard, we cut each at its own height. Sandy topsoil on a bank does not wait around once the grass thins, which is why we do not scalp the high spots.

If a bank keeps scalping, sliding or going bare, we say so while it is still a small problem. Often the better answer is a bed or ground cover instead of turf you cannot safely mow. Most yards go weekly from late March through October and every other week as growth slows. Both the Gregg County side and the Rusk County side of the lake are a short run from Longview, and the crew that learns your corners is the crew that comes back.

faq.q: What do you do with banks too steep to mow?
faq.a: We string-trim them. A mower on a wet bank is a safety problem, and a scalped bank washes. If a slope fights you every week, we will walk it with you and suggest a bed, ground cover or a short wall so you are not trimming it forever.

faq.q: How much does weekly mowing cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Typical yards start at $65 per visit. Lot size, how much slope and trimming there is, and how often you want us out all move it. You get a flat per-visit price in writing before the first mow, so there is nothing to guess at.

faq.q: Do you mow both sides of the lake?
faq.a: Yes. Lake Cherokee runs along the Gregg and Rusk county line, and we mow on both sides. The drive from Longview is short, so a regular weekly or bi-weekly slot works fine. Whichever shore you are on, you get the same crew, the same schedule and the same flat per-visit price in writing.

faq.q: Will clippings end up in the lake?
faq.a: Not if we can help it. We blow clippings back onto the lawn and clear the drive and walks, instead of pushing them downhill. Nothing is left piled against a wall or over a drain inlet where rain can carry it off.

faq.q: Can you cut shady grass under my pines lower to keep it neat?
faq.a: No, and it would hurt the lawn. Shaded St. Augustine stays at three and a half to four inches all summer. Cut short under the trees, it thins and the soil on a slope loses its cover. We cut each section at the height its grass needs.

leaf-removal.h1: Leaf and pine needle cleanup at Lake Cherokee
leaf-removal.lede: On a Lake Cherokee lot the leaves do not stay where they fall. We get them out of the lawn, beds and drains and haul them off the property.
leaf-removal.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes clears leaves and pine needles from Lake Cherokee yards, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We blow everything onto a paved surface, vacuum it with the area's only leaf vacuum trailer and haul it off with no bags. Pricing is one flat rate, quoted up front after a free walkthrough. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
leaf-removal.local_h: Where the leaves go on a lake lot
local: On flat ground a leaf drop is a chore. On a lake lot it is a moving problem. The pines and hardwoods around Lake Cherokee drop onto a slope, and every gust and every rain sends the pile a little further down the yard. It stacks against retaining walls, packs into beds and settles over drain inlets, where it blocks the water you are counting on to leave the lot.

That is why our cleanup is not just a blow-off. We clear the lawn, the beds and the drive, then clean out the drain inlets and the base of any wall where leaves collect. The crew works the debris onto the driveway or another paved surface the trailer can reach. Our leaf vacuum shreds it about 10 to 1, so roughly 10 yards of leaves hauls away as 1 yard. Nothing is bagged, and nothing gets blown downhill.

Timing follows the trees. Sweetgums let go in the first half of November and the volume jumps in a few days. Post oaks and water oaks keep dropping into February, so most lots want a pass in mid-November, another in mid-December and a last one before spring green-up. Pine needles fall more or less all year, and a lot with heavy pine cover may need an extra visit. We set the dates with you at the walkthrough, so the crew arrives after the drop and not before it.

Wet leaves on a lawn are worth taking seriously. If you have St. Augustine under the hardwoods, a damp mat in November can set up large patch, and the dead circles show up in March. Leaving it to wash off the slope is not a plan. Pricing depends on tree cover and how steep the lot is, and you get one flat number in writing before we start. With shredding and haul-off, the pile is gone for good.

faq.q: Do you keep leaves out of the lake?
faq.a: We collect leaves and haul them off site instead of blowing them downhill. We also clear drain inlets and the base of walls, where leaves pile up and block water. The goal is that nothing leaves the property toward the shoreline.

faq.q: How much does leaf removal cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: It is one flat price for the job, quoted in writing after a free walkthrough. Tree cover, how steep the lot is, how deep the leaves are and how many passes you want all move it. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter running.

faq.q: Can you clean pine needles out of my beds?
faq.a: Yes. We blow needles and leaves out of shrub beds and rock beds, vacuum them up and re-edge the bed lines they buried. Needles settle into everything on a slope, so beds and the lawn edge get the same attention as the open grass.

faq.q: How many passes will my lot need?
faq.a: Most lots do well with a pass in mid-November, one in mid-December and a last one before spring green-up. A lot under heavy canopy or full of oaks may need more. We plan the passes with you at the walkthrough.

faq.q: Do you clear gutters too?
faq.a: Exterior gutter clearing is part of our leaf work. Needles and leaves from the trees around the lake collect there as well, and a clogged gutter sends roof water down the slope where it does not belong. Gutter clearing can be added to the same visit as the lawn and beds, so the roof is clear when the next storm arrives.

mulch-installation.h1: Mulch that stays put on Lake Cherokee beds
mulch-installation.lede: Mulch on a slope wants to wash downhill. We pick the material and the edge that keep it in the bed at Lake Cherokee.
mulch-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes mulches beds at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We re-cut the edges, pull weeds by the root, loosen the soil and lay mulch or pine straw 1 to 1.5 inches deep. Most beds run $600 to $2,400, depending on how many beds and yards of mulch. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
mulch-installation.local_h: Choosing mulch for a bed that tilts
local: Shredded hardwood mulch floats. On a flat bed that is fine. On a steep lake bed, a heavy rain lifts it and carries it down the bank, and a few storms later the bed is bare and the lawn below is covered. Washed-out mulch is a common problem on a steep lake bed. So we choose material by the slope, not by habit. A bed that sheds its mulch every spring is a bed that needs a different plan.

Pine straw is usually the better choice on a steep bed. The needles knit together and stay put where a bark mulch would wash. It also looks right under pines. On flatter ground near the house, shredded hardwood works well. Either way it goes down 1 to 1.5 inches deep over a prepped bed, with an edge on the low side that keeps it in. Cypress, cedar and dyed mulch are options too.

If a bed keeps losing its mulch even after a better material and a firm edge, the mulch is not the problem. The bed is likely taking runoff from the slope above it, and that needs a drainage fix, not another truckload. We tell you so at the walkthrough. We do not put fabric under mulch, because mulch should turn into soil, and fabric stops that. Fixing the water beats adding another layer.

The best windows are late April through mid-May and late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop. Needles and leaves from the trees around the lake pile into beds, so we clear them first. Three inches is the calculator answer. In East Texas it sheds rain and rots stems, so we lay half that. Bed refreshes mostly run $600 to $2,400. We keep the edge crisp so the bed reads clean from the road.

Small habits keep beds healthy. We pull mulch back off stems and tree trunks so nothing rots, and we loosen the crusted top inch of soil so rain reaches the roots instead of running off. A 2,000 square foot bed takes about 8 yards at our depth, against 19 at three inches. Less mulch, laid right, also means less to wash downhill, and you only pay for what the beds actually need.

faq.q: Why does my mulch keep washing out at the lake?
faq.a: Slope and water. Hardwood mulch floats and slides off a steep bed in a heavy rain. Pine straw holds better, and an edge on the low side keeps it in. If the bed is taking runoff from above, that needs a drainage fix too.

faq.q: How much does mulching cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most beds run $600 to $2,400. The price follows square footage, the number of beds, the type of mulch and how much edging and weed pulling the beds need. A thin fall top-dress costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: Is pine straw or hardwood mulch better on a slope?
faq.a: Pine straw on steeper beds, because it knits together and stays put. Shredded hardwood on flatter ground near the house. We can use either, and we will recommend one per bed after seeing the grade. If a bed is borderline, a thin top-dress of pine straw over the old layer is often enough.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be?
faq.a: One to 1.5 inches. More than that sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover. We keep it pulled back off stems and trunks. Piled deeper against a trunk, it traps moisture and invites rot.

faq.q: Do you clear leaves before you mulch?
faq.a: Yes. We pull weeds and light debris, re-cut the edges and loosen the top inch of soil first. Mulch over a bed full of needles and old growth does not sit right, and it holds water against the plants. Clearing first also lets us spot bare roots and thin soil before they are buried.

retaining-walls.meta: Retaining walls at Lake Cherokee, TX, including rebuilds of leaning block walls with drainage behind them. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000.
retaining-walls.h1: Retaining walls built to drain at Lake Cherokee
retaining-walls.lede: Walls that hold a lake bank or a driveway cut, with a compacted base and drainage behind the block so water does not push it over.
retaining-walls.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes builds and rebuilds retaining walls at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We use segmental block, stone, boulder and timber on a compacted base with a drain behind every wall. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
retaining-walls.local_h: Holding a bank, and the driveway wall we rebuilt
local: In July 2026 we rebuilt a leaning block wall along a Lake Cherokee driveway. The wall had no real drainage behind it, which is the usual reason walls lean. We pulled the block out down to the ground, compacted a new base and set the wall back up course by course, with drainage fabric and pipe behind it. A gravel drain strip runs along the driveway side. Water now has a way out instead of pushing on the block.

A driveway cut into a bank puts steady pressure on whatever holds it up. Lake Cherokee lots fall to the water, so a wall may hold the drive, the yard above or the soil beside a house. Sandy topsoil over clay will not carry a wall set on undisturbed dirt. So we excavate below grade, compact crushed stone, set the first course dead level and backfill with gravel, with a perforated drain at the bottom and an outlet.

Not every slope needs one big wall. On a steep grade, terraced walls that step down the bank can hold more than a single tall one, and they leave room for planting. Short seating and garden walls start at a few thousand dollars. Taller walls get geogrid reinforcement, and if a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough. Tell us what the slope does after a hard rain, because that decides the drainage.

One boundary: a wall that holds your yard is our work, and a seawall at the water's edge is not. We rebuild leaning or failed walls when they can be saved. Some are too far gone and need a new design, and we will tell you which after we look. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, set by height, length and drainage, and the estimate is in writing. You see it in writing before any dirt moves.

faq.q: Can a leaning retaining wall be fixed?
faq.a: Often, yes. On the Lake Cherokee driveway wall we rebuilt in July 2026, we took the block down, compacted a new base and rebuilt it course by course with drainage fabric and pipe behind it. Some walls are too far gone, and we will tell you which after we look.

faq.q: Why do retaining walls lean?
faq.a: Water, almost always. East Texas clay swells when wet, and behind a wall with no drain the water builds pressure until the block leans and bows. A weak base is the second cause. We build a drain and a compacted base into every wall.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, depending on height and length. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls on a steep bank can run $20,000 or more. We price yours after walking the slope.

faq.q: Do you build seawalls or bulkheads?
faq.a: No. Seawalls, docks and boathouses are not our work, and a shoreline specialist should handle them. We build the walls on the land side that hold the yard, the drive and the slope. If the bank at the water's edge is what you need fixed, we can say where our work stops and theirs starts, and we will not take on a job we should not.

faq.q: Does a tall wall need an engineer?
faq.a: Sometimes. If a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough, before you commit to a price. Taller walls also get geogrid reinforcement as part of the build. It depends on height, the soil behind it and what sits above it. We do not guess on that part.

sod-installation.title: Lake Cherokee Sod Installation on Slopes | Yard Dog
sod-installation.meta: Sod installation at Lake Cherokee, TX. Cover bare, washing ground fast, pinned on steeper grades. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet.
sod-installation.h1: Sod to hold bare ground at Lake Cherokee
sod-installation.lede: Sod holds soil the day it goes down, which is why it is the fast fix for bare, washing ground on a gentle Lake Cherokee slope.
sod-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes lays sod at Lake Cherokee from our base in Longview, a short drive southeast. We strip old turf, level and amend the soil, and install bermuda, St. Augustine or Zoysia with tight seams and a watering plan. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
sod-installation.local_h: Putting turf back on a bank that has washed
local: Seed on a slope washes out with the first hard rain. Sod does not, because it arrives as a mat with roots already in it. That is the reason we lean on sod for bare ground at Lake Cherokee. Once the grass thins on a lake bank, sandy topsoil leaves quickly, and every storm takes a little more. A fresh mat of turf stops the loss right away, so the lot is not leaking into the water all spring.

Prep decides whether it stays. We strip old turf and weeds to bare soil, set the grade and till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil. On a gentle grade the sod is laid with staggered seams, tight to the edges. On steeper grades we pin it in place so it cannot slide before it roots. Past a certain angle, no grass holds, and a bed or a short wall is the better answer.

Shade under the trees picks the grass, not price. For sun we usually lay Tif419 bermuda. In the filtered light under pines and hardwoods it is St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on how much shade tolerance the spot needs. Under about four hours of sun no turf thrives long-term, and that corner is better as a shade bed or mulch. Bermuda in shade thins to dirt by August.

Timing is bermuda from late April through August and St. Augustine from May through September, in by the end of September so it gets four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy. Watering is half the job. New sod needs a deep morning soak daily for two weeks, then a taper. You get that schedule in writing. Pallet pricing puts most jobs between $1,500 and $4,700. Skip the soak in July heat and a new install can brown out in two weeks.

faq.q: Will sod hold on my sloped lake yard?
faq.a: On a gentle slope, yes, especially once it is rooted. On steeper ground we pin it in place until the roots take. Past a certain grade, a bed or a wall will hold better than any grass. We tell you at the walkthrough which parts of the yard are sod ground and which are not.

faq.q: How much does sod cost at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet. Square footage, grass type, removal of old turf, grading and access for pallets change the number. Small patch repairs cost less. You get the quote in writing before we start.

faq.q: What grass should I put under my pines?
faq.a: St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on shade. Bermuda quits in shade. If a spot gets under about four hours of sun, no turf will do well long-term, and a shade bed or mulch fits better. We map the sun first, because a lake lot often has shade on one side and open sky on the other. A split of two grasses is common.

faq.q: Can you do a small patch instead of the whole yard?
faq.a: Yes. We do patch repairs, plugs and full-yard installs. A washed-out strip along a drive or a bare slope by a wall is a common patch job, and we match the grass already there. Before we patch, we look at why the spot washed out, because new sod in the same conditions fails the same way.

faq.q: How do I water new sod?
faq.a: A deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks, then taper to deeper, less frequent soaks as the roots take hold. Skip it in July heat and a new install can brown out fast. Our written schedule walks you through it.

tree-planting.title: Lake Cherokee Tree Planting on Slopes | Yard Dog Landscapes
tree-planting.meta: Tree planting at Lake Cherokee, TX: level shelf on the slope, wide hole, watering basin and mulch ring. Species picked for wet or dry ground. Free quote.
tree-planting.h1: Planting trees on Lake Cherokee slopes
tree-planting.lede: A new tree on a lake slope needs a level shelf, the right species for how wet its spot stays and a watering plan that works.
tree-planting.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes plants trees at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We pick a species for the spot, dig a wide hole, set the root flare at grade and build a watering basin and mulch ring. Planting is quoted after a free walkthrough because the tree drives the cost. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-planting.local_h: Setting a tree on a lot that tilts to the water
local: Plant a tree straight into a slope and the water goes around the root ball, not into it. At Lake Cherokee we cut a level planting shelf first. The hole is dug wide and shallow, the basin is built up on the downhill side, and a mulch ring goes on off the trunk. Rain and hose water soak in where the roots are, instead of running past on the way to the shore.

A single Lake Cherokee lot can hold very different ground. Low on the lot, the soil stays wet and a bald cypress handles it well. Up the slope the ground drains fast and dries out, and native oaks do well in the open. In the shade of the existing pines, redbuds and dogwoods fit. We match each tree to how wet or dry its spot stays, not to what is available at the nursery that week.

Fall is the best time here, from September until around Thanksgiving. Soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools, so an October tree gets close to six months of root growth before summer. A new tree drinks from its root ball, and in July that ball can dry out in about a day and a half while the clay beside it stays moist. On a sunny, windy bank we also stake.

Sandy topsoil over clay is why watering advice matters. Soak the ball itself on a slow trickle for about twenty minutes, twice a week for six weeks on a fall tree, then weekly through November. Bigger installs get a check-in around the 30-day mark. Because species, size and access all change the cost, we quote after walking the slope. You get all of it in writing, so the plan is not just in your head.

Mulch and a basin finish the job. The mulch ring goes on off the trunk, never piled against it, and the basin holds a slow soak right where the roots are. We would usually rather plant a smaller tree that roots in fast than a big one that sulks. Healthy stock comes from regional growers, and circling roots are cut before the tree goes in with native soil, not a pocket of bagged mix that turns into a bathtub on a wet slope.

faq.q: What trees grow well near the water at Lake Cherokee?
faq.a: Bald cypress handles wet ground low on a lot well. Up the slope, native oaks do well in the open, and redbuds and dogwoods fit in the shade of existing pines. We match each tree to how wet or dry its spot stays.

faq.q: Why do you plant on a level shelf?
faq.a: On a slope, water runs past the root ball instead of soaking in. A level shelf with a basin built up on the downhill side holds the water where the roots are. It also keeps the tree from leaning as it settles.

faq.q: How much does it cost to plant a tree?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size, number of trees, access and soil at the spot all matter. You get a written quote after a free walkthrough, with the aftercare plan included.

faq.q: When should I plant on the lake?
faq.a: Fall is best, September until around Thanksgiving. We plant year-round, but a spring tree gets far less root time before summer and needs more watering through its first July and August. Fall roots have close to six months before summer, and a spring tree has about eight weeks.

faq.q: Will the tree need staking?
faq.a: Only on windy, exposed sites. An open bank above the water can qualify. We stake when the wind calls for it and not as a habit. Stakes come out once the tree can stand on its own. A tree in a sheltered spot lower on the lot usually does fine without them, and we tell you which case yours is.

tree-shrub-care.meta: Tree and shrub pruning at Lake Cherokee, TX: shaping, low limbs lifted for the water view, small trees removed. Quoted after a free walkthrough.
tree-shrub-care.h1: Pruning trees and shrubs on Lake Cherokee lots
tree-shrub-care.lede: Shrubs shaped, low limbs lifted and small trees cleared on Lake Cherokee lots where tall pines and hardwoods crowd everything underneath.
tree-shrub-care.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes prunes trees and shrubs at Lake Cherokee, a short drive southeast of our Longview base. We shape shrubs, thin crepe myrtles, lift low limbs, remove small trees and shrubs, and haul off every cut. Large trees near the house belong to a tree service. Our part is quoted after a free walkthrough. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-shrub-care.local_h: Working under the pines and hardwoods
local: Lake Cherokee yards tend to have tall pines and hardwoods with shrubs crowding underneath. Years of shade leave the shrubs leggy, and the trees leave dead lower limbs hanging at head height. We walk the lot, identify each plant and flag what needs work and what should be left alone. You get a written quote after that, usually within a day. Nothing gets cut until you have seen the plan and the number.

A lot of the work here is about the view and the light. We lift low limbs that block the line to the water, thin shrubs that have grown into a wall and take out small trees and shrubs that have outgrown their spot. We cut at the branch collar, sized to what the plant can close over. On a slope we keep roots in mind, so a plant holding a bank gets thinned and not pulled.

Timing is set by species. Crepe myrtles and knockout roses go in February, azaleas right after bloom, and hollies and boxwoods in early summer. Oaks are the exception. East Texas has oak wilt, and the beetles that spread it are drawn to fresh cuts in spring and early summer, so we prune oaks in the dead of winter or late summer. A storm-broken oak limb is cut clean and sealed right away.

Big trees are where we draw the line. A tall pine or hardwood hanging over the house, or limbs high in the canopy, are work for a tree service, and we will tell you so at the walkthrough. We handle what we can reach and do properly, then rake up and haul off every limb and trimming before we leave. Anything we are not sure we can do properly, we say so up front instead of guessing on a limb over your roof.

Storms are part of lake work too. When limbs come down onto lawns, beds and slopes, we handle the storm cleanup and haul everything off, and we clear dead lower limbs from shade trees while we are there. Seasonal feeding for trees and shrubs and a mulch refresh around tree bases are on our list as well, so the ground under the canopy gets attention along with the branches. Recovery pruning on a badly cut tree is planned over several winters.

faq.q: Can you open up the view to the lake?
faq.a: Within limits. We can lift low limbs, thin shrubs and remove small trees that block the view. Big trees and limbs high in the canopy are work for a tree service, and we will say so at the walkthrough. Show us the view line from the deck or porch and we will work to it.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost?
faq.a: We do not publish a price because the work varies so much from yard to yard. It depends on the number of plants, their size and condition, and what each needs. You get a written, itemized quote after a free walkthrough.

faq.q: When is the right time to prune on the lake?
faq.a: Late winter is the main window. Crepe myrtles and knockout roses go in February, spring bloomers right after they flower, and oaks in winter or late summer, not spring. We schedule by species. Cutting at the wrong time costs you blooms, or on an oak, risks oak wilt, so the calendar matters as much as the cut.

faq.q: My crepe myrtle was topped. Is it ruined?
faq.a: Not always. Recovery takes two or three winters of thinning, and we plan it out and come back each dormant season. If the tree is the wrong size for its spot, a smaller variety is the real fix. Please do not top it again. Topping makes the tree grow back taller on weaker wood.

faq.q: Do you take away what you cut?
faq.a: Yes. Limbs, trimmings and sawdust are raked up and hauled off before we leave. We also do storm cleanup, so downed limbs after a blow are on the list. Everything leaves with us, so the slope below the tree is not left with a pile of cut limbs waiting for the next rain to move them.
